title: The tailor's accounting
hookLine: a tailor tells God: I sinned a little, You let children suffer; let us forgive each other

lines: A TAILOR WITH HIS OWN WAY.
TALKING TO GOD LIKE A PARTNER.
cards: Yom Kippur in Berditchev, hours into the fast. A crowded synagogue, people tapping their chests as they read the long lists of sins from the prayer book.
Among them, the story goes, is a tailor with his own way of doing this. He isn't reciting a list. He's talking to God, quietly, the way you'd talk to a business partner across a kitchen table.
Afterward the rebbe, Levi Yitzchak, asks him what he said. The answer is bold. The rebbe's reply is bolder.

teach.b: Here's what the tailor says, as the story is told. Master of the world, I've done wrong. Sometimes I kept the leftover scraps of cloth.
Once or twice I ate without washing my hands. Small things. But You have taken babies from their mothers, and mothers from their babies.

teach.h: YOU FORGIVE ME, I FORGIVE YOU.
teach.b: You forgive me, and I'll forgive You. Let's call it even. Can anyone talk to God like that?

Levi Yitzchak doesn't scold him. In the telling, the rebbe's only complaint is that the tailor settled too cheaply. With an argument like that, he says, you could have demanded that God redeem the whole Jewish people.
Why isn't this blasphemy? Because it stands in a very old line.
Abraham argued with God over Sodom: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Moses argued. Job argued for chapters.
The Hebrew word for an accounting is cheshbon, and the season before Yom Kippur is a time for cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul. The tailor simply turned the ledger both ways.
The story doesn't explain why children suffer.
Jewish tradition has wrestled with that question at least since Job, whose book never hands him a tidy explanation. This story doesn't pretend to have one. It refuses to fake it.
You only argue with someone you believe is listening.
And it closes a week of Hasidic tales: the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, and the tailor's accounting.

how: Hasidic communities retell stories like the tailor's around Yom Kippur, and many Jews make a cheshbon ha-nefesh, an honest accounting of the soul, in the weeks before the day.

o: an accounting, a reckoning of what's owed
a confession recited from a list of sins
a knot tied on the corner of a prayer shawl

games.q: who said what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: you forgive me, I forgive You
shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?

s: in the story, Levi Yitzchak scolds the tailor for his chutzpah
his only complaint is that the tailor settled too cheaply.
arguing with God has roots in the Hebrew Bible itself
Abraham argued over Sodom, and Moses and Job argued too.
the story explains why children suffer
it doesn't. it refuses to pretend there's an easy answer.

games.q: you're the rebbe. a tailor tells you the deal he offered God on Yom Kippur: I'll forgive You if You forgive me. what do you say?
games.why: in the story, Levi Yitzchak says the tailor could have demanded the redemption of the whole people. he pushes the argument further, not back.

practice: Let one thing come up that you've been too polite to say, to God if you pray, or to yourself, if that fits you better: a loss that made no sense, a hope that went unanswered, a hurt you keep covering with good manners.
You don't have to fix it or explain it. Just say it plainly, inside, the way the tailor did, and let it sit there, said.

wordCard.voice: Cheshbon, the Hebrew word for an accounting. A Yom Kippur bargain from Berditchev: You forgive me, I forgive You. Honesty, in the one place people expect only apology.

orig.note: Hebrew: an accounting of the soul, the stock-taking many Jews do before Yom Kippur.

carryVoice: Your line: let's call it even. An honest ledger runs both ways. Day three hundred one, done.
